t: receives lashes. If the seeds began to sprout from the ground, even if they have not yet taken hold in it by roots (Yad Peshutah, based on Responsa of the Rambam no. 564 regarding sowing on Shabbat).
one who weeds. Clearing weeds around a plant; he is treated as one who sows, since it helps growth.
one who covers. One who covers.
in a perforated pot. One who sows in it is like one who sows in the ground (Hilchot Terumot 5:15, where the size of the hole is explained).
rebellion lashes (makkat mardut). Lashes by rabbinic law.
it is forbidden to sow kilayim for a gentile. It is forbidden for a Jew to sow kilayim in a gentile's land in the Land of Israel, even for the gentile's needs.

and it is permitted to tell a gentile to sow kilayim of seeds for him. In the gentile's land, even if he sows for the Jew's benefit (Rik"u, Radbaz, Gra on Yoreh De'ah 297:7, Yad Peshutah; and see the poskim and opinions for further explanations).
words of tradition. Tradition of the Sages.
seeds. Plants.
the roots. The roots.
who grafted a scion of an apple tree onto an etrog tree. He stuck a detached branch of an apple tree into an etrog tree so that it would fuse with it and grow.

and it is forbidden for a Jew to leave the gentile etc.. Descendants of Noah are forbidden to graft trees (Hilchot Melakhim 10:6), and so it is forbidden for a Jew to allow a gentile to graft trees for him (Melekhet Shlomo, Gra on Yoreh De'ah 295:4, Yad Peshutah; compare below 9:2).
and it is permitted to plant a scion etc.. It is permitted to take a branch from a tree that was grafted in violation and plant it elsewhere.
and kusmin. Wild wheat (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:1).
and shibbolet shu'al and shifon. Kinds of wild barley (ibid.).
and they are every seed eaten by humans. Plants whose seeds are eaten.
and afunim. The cultivated chickpea plant, today called chumus.
and the safir. Pea; some identify it as the Egyptian cowpea or French bean.
and the fruit of that seed is human food. Its edible part, such as the tuber or the leaves.
the chatzir. Leek, called in the language of the Sages 'karishah' (based on Targum Onkelos on Numbers 11:5 and Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 17:5).

and flax seed is included among garden seeds. Although it differs from other garden seeds, since flax is not human food but is used for making threads, whereas the seed itself is sometimes used for eating (Yad Peshutah).
and trados. Leaf beet (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:3).
and kusbar. Coriander.
and karpas. Celery or a similar variety.
and maror. Very bitter wild lettuce (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 2:6).
se'ah. About 7 liters.
two kavs of barley, two kavs of lentils and two kavs of beans. A total of six kavs, which is a se'ah.
and he shall sort. He shall sort out from the wheat.
but garden seeds etc.. For garden seeds we do not measure by the quantity of seed but by the area sown.

of what is sown in a beit se'ah of that kind. A beit se'ah is an area suited to sowing a se'ah of wheat (fifty cubits by fifty cubits, about 625 sq. m.). For sowing garden seeds this area suits other quantities of seed, as he explains below.
and mustard, one sows a kav of it in each beit se'ah. In terms of area sown, a kav of mustard equals a se'ah of grain.

if half a kav of it got mixed into each se'ah of grain or legumes, he should reduce. Half a kav is one twelfth of a se'ah, and when he sows this mixture the secondary seed will occupy one twenty-fourth of the area.
three quarters in each se'ah. Three quarters of a kav of flax seed in a se'ah of grain, a ratio of one to eight.

when he did not intend to mix, and when he did not intend to sow the two kinds that got mixed. For that is the nature of seed, that it has a little waste that is not cared about, and everything is considered one kind.
but if he intended to mix seed with other seed or to sow the two kinds etc.. When he wants the other kind sown, it is not considered natural waste and is forbidden as kilayim.
a heap of barley. A pile of barley seeds.
grain and legumes in grain and legumes. A kind of grain or legume that grew within another kind of grain or legume.
or garden seeds in grain and legumes and in garden seeds. A kind of garden seed that grew within grain or legumes or within another kind of garden seed.
the aftergrowth of astis. Aftergrowth is what grows on its own after the plant is harvested, and astis is a plant from which a blue dye is made.

and fenugreek that he sowed for human food etc.. Tiltan is the plant called today fenugreek (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 2:5). When fenugreek is sown for human food, the weeds hinder its growth, and he would not be suspected of sowing them with the fenugreek intentionally (unlike fenugreek sown for animal food; see Babylonian Talmud Bava Kamma 81a).
a boundary all around. A fence.
the place of threshing floors. Where grain is gathered after harvest.
that came up. That grew.
for he does not want a plant to grow in the place of threshing floors. The place must be smooth for threshing grain (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 2:5).

one does not plant vegetables inside the sedan of a sycamore. A sedan is a tree trunk whose branches were cut off (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 4:8), and a sycamore is a wild fig (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:1). Although the vegetable does not fuse with the sycamore, it is forbidden because it resembles grafting a vegetable onto a tree (see above 1:5).
even under a grapevine. Although kilayim in a vineyard is more severe (as below 5:4).
for he does not want their taking root. He placed them in the manner of burying (a bundle with some leaves exposed), not in the manner of sowing.
he is concerned for kilayim. Because there is a resemblance to grafting, since the turnip and radish penetrate the roots of the tree (Arukh HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 297:20).
and the roots remained in the ground. Roots remained that are visible from the outside (Derekh Emunah, Yad Peshutah in its first explanation).
he shall not sow etc.. Even if he will manage to sow and harvest before the first plants sprout again, because of appearance (ibid.).
and he changed his mind to sow it with barley. He regretted sowing wheat and decided to sow barley.
and they will rot. They will decay.
about three days if his field was moist. When the field is moist, the seeds usually rot within three days. When the field is dry the process takes longer (Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 2:2).

as they plow it before the rain so that it will be moistened. Before the rain they turn the soil slightly so that the rain will penetrate to its depth; it is a light plowing without precision (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 2:3).

it is permitted to sow there another kind. Since the wheat will not grow again after the animal grazed it (Derekh Emunah, unlike what was cited above in halakhah 12, where it speaks of kinds that tend to grow again).
on the first of Adar etc.. The time when the crop begins to grow (Rashi, Megillah 13b).
they announce. They proclaim.
at first they used to etc.. The court's emissaries used to uproot the kilayim, and field owners were lazy to do so themselves before the fifteenth of Adar.
but less than this, they should not touch it. For there is no obligation to uproot, as above 5:7.
and they go out in the intermediate days of the festival of Passover. See also Hilchot Yom Tov 7:11.
the late crop. The late one, crops that are late in growing.
that have sprouted. That began to grow.
we do not wait for them. Until the intermediate days of the festival (Babylonian Talmud Mo'ed Katan 6a, according to the commentary of R. Chananel).

since they are one kind. They have equal natural properties (as below halakhah 5), such as nutritional values (Chazon Ish, Kilayim 3:1), growing conditions (ibid. section 7), or natural propagation from one another (Yad Peshutah). However, we do not have a precise definition of how plants are divided into kinds (see further below halakhah 6 in the poskim and opinions).
chazeret with chazeret of the hills. Cultivated lettuce with mountain lettuce.
and endives with field endives. Cultivated chicory with common chicory.
and leeks with field leeks. Leek with a kind of wild garlic (some identify it with a plant called tall garlic).
and kusbar. See above 1:9.
and gourd (dela'at). The bottle gourd, called kra in Aramaic and Arabic.
the roasted gourd. A very bitter gourd fit for eating only after being buried in hot ashes called ramatz (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:2).

the zonin. A kind of inferior wheat that changed from other wheat (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:1). Apparently this refers to the weed called darnel, which grows with wheat and whose grains resemble its grains.
shibbolet shu'al... and kusmin... the shifon... the safir. See above 1:8.

and the purkadan with the tofach. The purkadan is identified with a cultivated tofach, whose seeds resemble peas. The tofach is apparently one of its varieties. In the Commentary on the Mishnah (ibid.) he wrote that its grains are white, round and hard.

and the white bean with the se'u'it. The se'u'it is the cultivated cowpea (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.), and the white bean is apparently one of its varieties (some identify it with the climbing bean).
and the kishut. The snake melon, resembling a large cucumber (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 1:2).
the tarbutor. Wild cabbage with thin stalks (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 1:3), apparently today's cauliflower.
and the trados. Leaf beet (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
the le'unin. Cultivated sorrel or cultivated orach.
the nafus. A variety of radish (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:5), which some identify with rutabaga (from which canola oil is made).
the lafsan. Field mustard.
the chuzrar. Some identify it with the Syrian pear.
and the afarksin. Peaches, which at the start of their growth resemble almonds (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:4).
and the shezafin. Cultivated jujube (not the fruit called plum).
the rimin. Apparently this refers to the common jujube.
pears with krustemelin. Some identify them with plums and apricots, and some with cultivated pears and one of their varieties.
and the perishin. Quinces.
the uzrarin. A light fruit resembling a small apple, growing on the thorny hawthorn shrub.
and likewise there etc.. In certain cases the Sages ruled that two kinds of different nature are considered one kind regarding kilayim, because there is a great external resemblance between them.

since the taste of this fruit is very far from the taste of that fruit. A great difference in taste can be a deciding consideration in defining two kinds regarding kilayim. It turns out that the decision in each individual case depends on weighing several factors: equal nature, external resemblance in leaves or fruit, and taste of the fruit.
according to the size of the field being sown. In a small field mixing is not visible even if he distances a little.
and the sending out of the shoots. The spreading of the tender branches.
a beit rova. An area suited to sowing a quarter-kav of wheat, that is one twenty-fourth of a beit se'ah.

about ten and a half cubits by ten and a half cubits square. This is an approximate measure, and in some versions a more precise measure appears: 'about ten and a fifth cubits by ten and a fifth cubits' (see R. Y. Shilat's note in Rambam Meduyak), which is about 26 sq. m.

whether in the middle or on the side. He must leave a vacant square area of this size in the middle of the border between the fields, or at the edge of the border. For the rest of the border's length he does not need such a distance, but must keep six handbreadths away (Yad Peshutah).
even a gourd. Whose leaves are long and tangle (below, halakhah 13).
six handbreadths. About 48 cm.
he keeps a beit rova between them. As above, halakhah 9.
a furrow. A trench.

its length is only six handbreadths. For that is where the division between the field and the row is recognizable. For the rest of the row's length he should keep a handbreadth between it and the field without a furrow (Yad Peshutah).

and its width like its depth. If the furrow's depth is one handbreadth, its width too must be a handbreadth, and so on if its depth is more than a handbreadth (but less than a handbreadth is not considered a furrow - Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah, and so it is implied below 4:4).
he keeps six handbreadths between them. Along the entire row (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah).

and needless to say etc.. This refers to above halakhah 12: the distance required between a vegetable field and a vegetable row is certainly sufficient when sowing a vegetable row next to a vegetable row (but between a row of grain and a row of vegetables he must keep six handbreadths - Derekh Emunah; see Radbaz, who explained differently).
as will be explained. Below 4:1, and see also below 4:10.
for it spreads a lot. It has large leaves that tangle with the crop beside it, and it looks like kilayim (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 2:11).
as we have explained. In the previous halakhah.
a bur. Ground that has not been plowed.
a nir. Ground that has been plowed but not sown.
a gapah. A hedge (from 'hagafat hadelet', Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 6:2).

a tree that screens the ground with its body. Its branches lean toward the ground and cover it, and the distance between them and the ground is less than three handbreadths (Radbaz, R. Y. Kafah and others, based on Tosefta Kilayim 2:5).

because the barley in his field appeared to be the end of his fellow's field. His field, which is sown with wheat next to barley, looks like a field of two people, since his barley looks like part of his fellow's field sown with barley.
for it is not the way of people to sow one furrow of flax. For it yields no usable produce (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 2:7).

and it turns out he is like one sowing to destroy. One who sows to test the field usually uproots the plant when it begins to grow, and has the law of one who sows a kind that is not customarily kept, where sowing it has no kilayim prohibition (Derekh Emunah).
it is forbidden to sow another kind. Even though he is sowing to test the field, since onlookers will think he is sowing for the use of the crop (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

two kinds of grain, he shall not sow mustard between them etc.. Although mustard resembles flax in the manner of its sowing, since a whole field is sown with it (as above 1:9), nevertheless since sometimes one furrow is sown with it, it has the law of other kinds that are forbidden to sow between grain fields even when his intent is only to test them, as brought in the previous halakhah.
and chari'a. Safflower.

it is permitted to sow mustard or chari'a between them. For testing them as brought in the previous halakhah. And onlookers will not think he is sowing for use, since mustard and chari'a harm vegetables.
to surround. To border.
a corner. The corner of the field.
a corner of one seed touching a side of the other seed. See the diagram.
a corner of one seed touching a corner of the other seed. See the diagram.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 16.

it is permitted to sow two rows side by side etc.. Each row four cubits wide (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 3:6), so each kind is sown in an area eight cubits wide (about 4 meters), and it looks like a small field (ibid. 3:4).
cucumbers... gourds. For their identification see above 3:3.
Egyptian bean. A kind of legume found only in Egypt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 7:2). Some identify it with a cultivated cowpea of a climbing variety.
and a furrow between each and every kind. For the measure of the furrow see above 3:12 (Yad Peshutah, based on Gra 297 note 36).
because these kinds etc.. Unlike other vegetables, which may be sown row beside row with a furrow between them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 3:4; see also above 3:12-13).
gourds. This halakhah is specifically about the gourd, whose leaves spread widely (Rik"u, Radbaz).
he uproots from the vegetable the place in which he sows a row of gourds. Four cubits wide.
and leaves of the vegetable. That he does not uproot.
so that between every two rows of gourds there are twelve cubits. Of vegetable, and a furrow between the gourds and the vegetable.
but less than this. Less than twelve cubits of vegetable between two rows of gourds.
a beit rova. See above 3:9.

for they have spread over it and taken up a large place. Its leaves spread before the grain was sown. But if the grain was sown before the gourd, it suffices to keep six handbreadths away from the grain and sow the gourd, and if afterwards its leaves reach the grain he must uproot from the grain (above 3:13).
it counts from the measure. It is measured as part of the beit rova.
a water channel. A conduit.
that are a handbreadth deep. And their width equals their depth (as above 3:12).

one on the edge of the furrow from here etc.. One seed on the outer side of the furrow, and a second seed on the other outer side of the furrow, so the furrow separates between them. And a third seed in the bottom of the furrow inside, and the depth of the furrow separates it from the first and the second (Rik"u, Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
and it is permitted to plant two kinds etc.. This halakhah speaks of planting seedlings that have already begun to put out leaves (Derekh Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
and even a kishut and a gourd. Which have long, tangling leaves as above, halakhah 1.
provided that this kind leans etc.. That at the time of planting he leans the leaves of each kind to a different side.
a mesher. A long strip.
and narrows as it goes. After he kept two cubits by two cubits at the beginning of the strip, he may sow in a diagonal line and come closer in his sowing to the strip beside it.
until there remains between them at the end of the strip only a minimal amount. Until the diagonal line reaches right next to the neighboring strip.
for they look as though they were not sown in mixture. Like the law of a corner touching a side (above 3:18).
patch by patch of each kind. Square plots of different kinds.
a beit rova. An area suited to sowing a quarter-kav of wheat, which is about ten and a fifth cubits by ten and a fifth cubits (see above 3:9 in the explanation).
for the strip is long. And the division between strip and strip is more recognizable, therefore they required less distance (Derekh Emunah).
as we have explained. Above 1:9.
six handbreadths. About half a meter.

four kinds on the four sides of a bed. Next to each of its sides, in the middle of the side, or at the corners of the bed, so as to use the maximum area for sowing while keeping the two required conditions: a distance of a handbreadth and a half between kind and kind, and no more than five different kinds (this can be done in several ways, see the diagrams in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 3:1, and see two possibilities in the diagrams here).
in its width. In a vacant area.
without a furrow and without leaning. If he did not make a furrow at the side of the bed and did not lean the leaves inside it.

and even opposite the corners of a bed that have no seed. Even if he sowed inside the bed in the middle of its sides and left the corners (horns) of the bed vacant, it is forbidden to sow outside the bed near its corners.
six by six. Handbreadths.
a border of a handbreadth all around. A fence a handbreadth high (as below halakhah 14), and a handbreadth wide (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 85a).

three on each border and six in the middle. Twelve kinds on the border and six in the bed itself. The reason for the permission is that the border looks like a separate place, distinct from the bed, and so they permitted sowing in the bed itself more than five kinds (unlike halakhah 9), since with the border added the bed is larger than six by six (Derekh Emunah).
and he shall not sow a turnip head in the border lest it fill it. He shall not sow on the border a turnip tuber to take root and grow there, because its leaves might fill the border's area.
more than this he shall not sow. One may not sow more than eighteen kinds, even if he is careful to keep a handbreadth and a half apart, because they look sown in mixture.
kinds of seeds. From which fields are customarily sown (above 1:9).
as we have explained. Above, halakhot 9-12.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 12.
since it was sown in it. After sowing.
even six by six. Small beds of six by six handbreadths, in which one should not sow more than five kinds per bed (as above, halakhah 9).

and he makes in each bed five circles etc.. Here a novelty is taught: if he sows in the shape of circles, it is permitted to sow more than five kinds in a bed, and he need not even keep a distance between them.
four on its four sides and one in the middle. Four circles adjacent to the four sides of the bed in the middle of the sides, and a fifth circle in the center of the bed.
and he sows four other kinds in the four corners of a bed. In the form of squares, one square in each corner of the bed.
bare. Without seed.
separated from the corners. Separated from the squares sown in the corners of the bed.
if the circles were sown warp etc.. If he sowed inside the circles vertical rows, he should sow outside the circles horizontal rows.

for when there is a separation between the two kinds... as we have explained. Above, halakhot 9 and 12, regarding sowing several kinds in a small bed. However, when there are many kinds in a small bed that look mixed, they were concerned about appearance even when he keeps a distance (Rik"u, and as above halakhah 9).
he receives two sets of lashes. Two punishments of lashes, where for each punishment he receives thirty-nine lashes.
and a grape seed. The pit of a grape.
by a handful toss. He drops the three seeds from his hand all at once.
he covered. He covered.

kinbes and luf and the like, of the seeds that finish with the end of the vineyard's crop. Perennial vegetables that ripen together with the grapes. Perhaps this refers to the karbas mentioned in the Mishnah (Kilayim 2:5 according to some versions), identified with a perennial seasoning vegetable called cumin today. And luf is a kind of onion (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 6:10), a perennial wild plant from whose seeds an edible bulb develops, which reaches its final size after three years, in the time when the vine bears fruit.

but other seeds are forbidden by their words. The Sages also forbade other vegetables, because some vegetables are forbidden by the Torah, but kinds of seeds that are not vegetables are entirely permitted, as below 5:6. On the other hand, the five kinds of grain are all forbidden by the Torah (Rik"u, Radbaz, Chazon Ish, Kilayim 1:9, Yad Peshutah).
to sow vineyard kilayim outside the Land. See further below 8:13-14.

and they did not forbid kilayim of seeds. As above 1:3. It turns out there are three distinctions outside the Land: kilayim of seeds are permitted, vineyard kilayim are forbidden by rabbinic law, and kilayim of trees are forbidden by the Torah (above 1:5).
forbidden for benefit. It is forbidden to benefit from them, as below, halakhah 7.

and one does not hoe with a gentile in kilayim. In kilayim of seeds in the Land of Israel, even in the gentile's own field, because a gentile cannot acquire so as to remove the sanctity of the Land (Hilchot Terumot 1:10). And in vineyard kilayim, both in the Land and outside it, even in the gentile's vineyard (Radbaz, Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah, as implied by this halakhah's proximity to the previous one).

but one uproots with him to reduce the tiflah. Some explain that it is permitted to uproot some of the plants with him, though the gentile intends the benefit of the remaining plants, since in the end he reduces the amount of kilayim. Others explain that the permission is only when he uproots everything, and the novelty is that it is permitted to do so even though for now he wants the kilayim he has not yet reached to remain so that he will get payment for uprooting them (both explanations are brought in Meiri, Avodah Zarah 64a).
the tiflah. Something improper.
other kinds of seeds. For example garden seeds from which fields are sown (above 1:9; regarding legumes see below halakhah 19 and the poskim and opinions there).
and needless to say other trees. 'For you have no kilayim in trees except grafting alone' (above 1:6).

it is forbidden to sow vegetables or grain beside the vines etc.. Although the liability of lashes is only for one who sows two kinds with a grape seed by a handful toss (as above, halakhah 2), in sowing that is not by a handful toss there is a Torah prohibition without lashes even for a single kind (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah; see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:6).
he has made it sanctified (kiddesh). The crops became forbidden ('sanctified' here is in the sense of removal and separation).

and they burn both of them, as it says 'lest it be sanctified (tikdash)'. The Sages expounded by tradition that the word 'tikdash' also means 'be set on fire' (Babylonian Talmud Kiddushin 56b; Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 8:1).
and left them. He did not uproot them.
and a person cannot sanctify something that is not his. He cannot impose a prohibition on what is not his property (see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1, Hilchot Shechitah 2:21).
in the seventh year. In a shemittah year, when all fields are ownerless and considered not his.

and maintained it. That he did not notify the vineyard owner (Radbaz); others explain that he performed an act that helps their growth (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah, in contrast to maintaining by the vineyard's owner, whose even inaction counts as maintaining, as brought at the beginning of the previous halakhah).
as we have explained. At the beginning of the previous halakhah.
the oppressor. A robber who seizes land.

if the owners were forgotten. If the vineyard's owner is hiding in fear of the oppressor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 7:6); it may also be explained that the owners were forgotten, meaning the field is no longer called by his name (Rash, ibid.; see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:6).

even though they have not despaired, it is sanctified by the Torah. In such a situation, where the robber can do as he wishes with the land, we do not say that a person cannot forbid what is not his (see Yad Peshutah).

even though they despaired, he sanctifies only by rabbinic law. The Sages decreed that even where the field is still called by the owner's name the robber sanctifies it, because the land appears to be in his ownership (Derekh Emunah), but by the Torah he does not sanctify, since the land is not acquired by him even if there was despair (see Hilchot Gezelah 8:14).

the wind that uprooted the branches of the vine and cast them onto the grain. That broke the vine's branches and dropped them on the grain (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 7:7), with the branches still partly attached to the vine (Rik"u and Radbaz).
he shall scrape. He shall remove.
and if an accident befell him. That he could not remove them.
when the oppressor leaves, he shall reap the seed immediately. If the oppressor left the vineyard, the vineyard owner must immediately reap the kilayim.
even on the intermediate days of a festival. When it is generally forbidden to reap, here they permitted it.
he shall add to them up to a third of their wage. For example, workers who usually receive thirty shekels an hour, he shall give them forty shekels (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 7:6).
they asked for more than this. More than a third over their wage.
he seeks gently and reaps. He looks for workers at the regular price, and in the meantime reaps little by little himself, to show that he does not want the kilayim to remain (ibid.).

and if the seed was delayed until it reached the time that it becomes sanctified. If he did not reap in the meantime and the stage of growth was reached at which the seed becomes forbidden, as explained in the next halakhah.
and both of them become forbidden. The seed and the vineyard.
from when they take root. From the moment the roots spread in the ground.
from when they become like a white bean. From when they have grown somewhat to the size of the legume called white bean (see above 3:3).

until this one sows. Regarding seeds (grain and vegetables) it says 'lest the full yield of the seed that you sow be sanctified' (Deuteronomy 22:9), meaning they become sanctified from the time of sowing, namely taking root.

and this one becomes produce. Regarding the vineyard it says 'and the produce of the vineyard', meaning it is sanctified from when it is called produce, that is when the grapes are somewhat fit for eating and are the size of a white bean (Derekh Emunah).

but grain that has dried as much as needed and grapes that have ripened as much as needed are not sanctified. Since they are called 'full yield of seed' or 'produce of the vineyard' only in the stages of growth, but at the end of growth they are already called wheat or grapes (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 7:7).

and if he uprooted the seed before the grapes became like a white bean, it is permitted for benefit. They did not decree regarding unripe grapes, and so if he uprooted the seed before the grapes grew to the size of a white bean, it is permitted to benefit from it (but if the grapes grew to the size of a white bean before he uprooted the seed, everything is forbidden by the Torah, as above halakhah 13).
and he picked the seed before it took root, it is permitted for benefit. Since before taking root it is not considered sown at all, the seed was not forbidden.

and if it took root, it is forbidden. Everything is forbidden by the Torah, as above halakhah 13 (the explanation of halakhot 14-15 follows Chazon Ish, Kilayim 3:21-23, as emerges from Rik"u in his conclusion, and similarly in the Gra's commentary on Yoreh De'ah 296 note 21).
as the vine dries in the cold days. As is the way of vines, whose leaves wither at the start of winter, though the vines themselves still have vitality and the ability to produce fruit.
and likewise one who sows in an unperforated pot etc.. See above 1:2.
and seeds fell from it. Without his knowledge.
or that came out with the manure or with the water. He fertilized his field or irrigated it and did not know that seeds were mixed in the fertilizer or the water.
winnowing. Scattering the grain in the wind to separate the husks.
in a field of lavan. In a field of grain.
and the wind blew them behind him. The wind blew seeds behind his back and he did not see.
and if he maintained them. That he did not uproot.
and how should he act etc.. They did not obligate him to search for the seeds immediately, but he may wait until he sees them growing (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
he turns them over with the plow and that suffices. It suffices to plow the area to prevent their growth.
and if he found that they had become aviv. If he did not notice the beginning of growth, but only after stalks with kernels grew and began to ripen.
he shall beat. He shall thresh (at this stage the crops are still moist and cannot be burned - Derekh Emunah).
grain. At the end of growth.

and if he saw them and maintained them, they shall be burned. By the law of one who maintains kilayim in a vineyard (above, halakhah 8). If he saw the kilayim growing and did not uproot them, he is like one who sowed with his hands deliberately, so the vines too must be burned (Radbaz, Yad Peshutah).

until he maintains something like which most of the people in that place maintain. That most people in that place are accustomed to sow it or wish it to grow in their fields (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 5:8).
in Arabia. In the lands of Arabia.
for they want thorns for their camels. It is customary there to let thorns grow with the human-food crop in order to feed them to camels (ibid.).
the iris. Mint (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 5:8); some explain it refers to the flower called today the iris.
and the ivy. Woodland ivy.
and the king's lily. According to the Rambam this is the anemone; some identify it with the white lily.
and all other kinds of seeds are not kilayim in a vineyard. As above 5:6.
and kinbes. Cultivated hemp.
and the kinras. Apparently the artichoke (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 1:6).
and tree wool. Cotton (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 7:2).
kinds of grasses. Leaf vegetables.
and the Egyptian bean. For its identification see above 4:1.
and the atadin. A kind of thorn that yields hard black grains fit for eating (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 7:5).
anything that puts out leaves from its root. Whose leaves grow or renew from the roots.
and anything that does not put out leaves from its root. But from the trunk or branches.
until it added one in two hundred. That it grew by half a percent.
he has sanctified. Like permitted food into which one part in two hundred of vineyard kilayim was mixed, where the entire food becomes forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 15:14).

consider this, if it dries up etc.. Try to understand the following case: if it dries out completely a hundred hours after picking, then in half an hour it loses half a percent of its moisture, and likewise in half an hour of attachment to the ground it gains half a percent in moisture (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 5:6).
it is forbidden to pass with a perforated pot etc.. There is a prohibition in the very carrying of the pot through a vineyard, but it becomes forbidden only if he set it on the ground under the vine.
and afterwards the onions grew from the planted root. The onions continued to grow permissibly from the root that had become forbidden.

even though the growths exceeded its root by two hundred. Even if the forbidden root is less than half a percent of the whole plant, so that it might seem that the root is nullified by being a minority.
for permitted growths do not release the forbidden root. The growths are permitted, but they have no power to nullify the prohibition of the root.
or one who maintains it until it added one in two hundred. He saw kilayim in a vineyard and they grew by half a percent from the time he saw them (as above 5:21).
sixteen cubits in every direction. About 8 meters on each side.

but if there was between them etc.. The previous halakhah said that the whole circle is seen as if full of vegetable, and below 7:1 it is explained that one must keep four cubits between a vineyard and another crop. Therefore four cubits are needed between the circle and the adjacent vine rows, and if there is no such distance, the circle is enlarged to the adjacent rows and every vine that enters the enlarged circle becomes forbidden.

and as if the width of the circle were forty cubits. If the rows are exactly four cubits from the circle, four cubits must be added on each side of the circle whose diameter is thirty-two cubits, so the diameter of the enlarged circle is forty cubits.
in the case of one who sows or maintains inside the vineyard. Since mixture is visible, a large area of the vineyard is forbidden.
and he was adjacent to it. He sowed adjacent to the vineyard, and did not keep the required distance of four cubits (below 7:1).
two rows of vines. Which have the law of a vineyard and are called 'produce of the vineyard' (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 4:5).

along the whole length of the seed and four cubits beyond the seed. Of the two rows next to the seed, all the vines planted parallel to the seed became forbidden, and likewise the vines planted four cubits beyond the seed on each side.

and four cubits' width is sanctified from the seed along the whole length of the vineyard row. A strip four cubits wide parallel to a row of vines (and if the rows of vines are shorter than the seed, they also forbade the seed four cubits beyond the vines on each side - Radbaz).
a single vine. An isolated vine, or several vines that do not have the law of a vineyard (as explained below 7:1-2).
in every direction. On each side of the vine.
a yalda less than a handbreadth. A vine whose trunk is lower than a handbreadth and from which shoots emerge on which the grapes grow.
does not sanctify the seeds. For it is not considered a vine.

when is this said? with two opposite two and one sticking out as a tail. Vines planted in this way are considered a small vineyard (see below 7:7 and diagram A there). However, for the law here they do not have the law of a sanctifying vineyard (and all the more so if they were planted in a way that has no vineyard law at all, as below 7:1).
two gardens one above the other. With a kind of step ('terrace') between them.

he sows the upper one until he reaches the airspace of ten handbreadths close to the vineyard. He may sow the upper one up to the edge and continue sowing on the slope descending to the vineyard, up to a distance of ten handbreadths from the top of the vines.
from the base of the vines. The trunk of the vines.
he turns the seeds over with the plow. And he must wait until the seeds rot or begin to sprout, as above 2:13-14 (Derekh Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
uprooting with the root. He uproots them with the root.
one who layers the vine in the ground. He bends a branch of it and buries it in the soil so that it will grow from another place.
a silon. A pipe.
and if there was less than this on top of it, it is forbidden to sow on top of it. Since at this depth the roots of the seed reach the vine's branch (Radbaz, based on the Jerusalem Talmud).
and it is permitted to sow beside it. Since roots go downward and do not reach the vine (ibid.).

it is permitted to bring seed onto it. Since the rock is hard and roots do not penetrate it. However, they required three finger-breadths of soil on top of the rock because of appearance (Derekh Emunah).
when is this said. That it is permitted to sow on top of the layering.
when the root of the vine is not visible. That he layered the entire vine in the ground and covered it completely (so that it would grow in another place).
but if its root was visible etc.. If he layered only the shoots of the vine and left the trunk exposed above the ground, he must keep a distance from the trunk.
as will be explained. Below 7:1.
and their roots are visible. That he layered only the shoots.
from four cubits to eight. The customary distance between vine and vine when planting a vineyard, as below 7:2.

these combine with the other standing vines, as if he had not layered them. They have the law of any row of vines that combines to form a vineyard (see below 7:1-2, that three vines are considered a row and two rows are considered a vineyard from which one must keep four cubits).
and if not, they do not combine. If there are less than four cubits between them or more than eight, they have the law of single vines from which one keeps only six handbreadths.

if there were fewer than three etc.. If there were only two layered vines, they do not combine with a regular vine to form a row, because layered vines are considered vines for combining into a vineyard only when they form a row by themselves, as at the beginning of the previous halakhah.
the branches. Thin shoots.

he trained the vine on part of the epifirot. Epifirot are reeds and the like from which he made a kind of frame or trellis (pergola), called an 'arisa', to rest the vine's shoots on (below 8:1). Here it speaks of one who set the vine on part of the area of the epifirot.

he shall not sow under the extension of the epifirot etc.. One should not sow under the continuation of the epifirot, even in a place with no shoots, because they were made for the vine to spread over all of them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 6:4).
it is permitted. For eating, but the seed must be uprooted since it was sown in violation (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
tree branches. Branches of a tree.
he returns them to another place. And they were not forbidden, since he sowed permissibly (Radbaz).

reeds that stick out from the trellis etc.. Reeds meant to support the lattice over which the vine is spread, and he refrained from cutting them for fear of damaging the reeds from which the lattice is made, not with the intention that the vine spread over them.
a shoot that comes out of the trellis. A young sprouting branch growing beyond the boundaries of the trellis or the trailing vine and hanging in the air.
the trailing vine (dalit). A single vine climbing a tree or fence and the like.
a plumb line. A string with a weight at the end, used as a level to straighten walls and pillars during construction (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 12:8).

four cubits... six handbreadths. These measures are called 'the work of the vineyard' or 'the work of the vine' (Mishnah Kilayim 6:1, Babylonian Talmud Eruvin 93a), for a vineyard needs four cubits around it for its work (for example for the passage of plowing oxen), and for a single vine six handbreadths suffice for its work.
and likewise if there was between them less than four, they are like one vine. For they lack proper growing conditions to grow beside one another.

and we see the middle one as if it were not there. The two outer rows, between which there are less than eight cubits, are considered together a vineyard, without taking into account the middle row separating them, since this row was not given a proper place for its growth and will end up uprooted (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 5:2).
and he keeps from each row only six handbreadths. The measure of distance from single vines that are not a vineyard.

he must keep four cubits from the outer row like other vineyards. Since a person standing outside does not notice the distance between the rows and it seems to him they are planted properly (Rik"u, Kesef Mishneh).
like a vineyard that was destroyed in its middle. Which has stringent distancing laws, as below halakhah 11.
for from the beginning he planted them far apart. And they never had the law of a vineyard.
a path for the public. A path on which many people pass (unlike 'the public thoroughfare', which is sixteen cubits wide, and with such a width the rows do not combine - Raavad's critique).
two opposite two and one sticking out like a tail. See diagram A.
this is called a small vineyard. For the fifth vine can be seen as completing the two rows, so that they are like two rows with three vines in each (R. Y. Kafah).
two opposite two and one in the middle. See diagram B.
or three in this row and two opposite them in the second row. Diagram C.
a vineyard that was destroyed etc.. A vineyard whose area is very large, and many vines were uprooted from it so that large empty areas remained in it.

if there is enough to gather ten vines per beit se'ah etc.. If ten vines can be found in an area suited to sowing a se'ah of wheat (about 625 sq. m.), and these vines are planted in the form of two small vineyards (as above, halakhah 7).

or there is enough to align three opposite three. That six vines can be found in the area of a beit se'ah (Rik"u), and these vines are planted in two parallel rows with three vines in each row (as a regular vineyard, as above halakhah 2).
a poor vineyard. A vineyard with few vines relative to its area, which nevertheless has the law of a vineyard over the entire area.

if there is enough to align two opposite three. That three vines can be found planted parallel to two vines, so that the five vines form something like two rows (the meaning of the Rambam's words is that this can be drawn in various ways - Yad Peshutah; others explain specifically in the way that the fifth vine 'sticks out like a tail' - Rik"u and Radbaz. The distance from vine to vine must be from four cubits to eight cubits, as above halakhah 2).
the roots were aligned. The trunks of the vines are planted parallel.
and the foliage. The branches and leaves.
thin ones. Vines with a thin trunk.
he brings the measuring cord and stretches it from this one to that. To check whether three vines are in one row; if all touch the stretched cord, it is a row (see Tosefta Kilayim 3:4).

if the clearing in its middle has sixteen cubits. Besides 'the work of the vineyard', which is the four cubits adjacent to the vines (above halakhah 1), there are four additional free cubits, and likewise on the other side of the clearing there are four cubits for the work of the vineyard and four additional cubits, for a total of sixteen cubits.

and if it does not have sixteen cubits, he shall not bring seed there. When there are not four free cubits on each side of the vines, this place is nullified to the vineyard, for a place without four cubits has no independent importance (Rashi, Eruvin 3b).

the machol of the vineyard. An area on which one forgoes (mochel) and gives up sowing (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 4:2). Others explain 'machol' from the sense of encircling (as in 'mecholot'), meaning the area around the vineyard (Rashi, Eruvin 3b; Rash and Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, Kilayim 4:2).

if it had less than twelve cubits, he shall not bring seed there. Since it is customary not to sow in the four cubits adjacent to the fence, and in the four cubits adjacent to the vines it is forbidden to sow, he is left with an area of less than four cubits for sowing, and such an area has no importance (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid., based on Eruvin 93a).

in a large vineyard... a small vineyard. A large vineyard is one with at least two rows with three vines in each row (as explained above, halakhah 1), while a small vineyard has five vines, two opposite two and one sticking out as a tail (as above, halakhah 7; Rik"u, R. Y. Kafah). Others explain that a large vineyard is one with three rows of three vines each, while the small vineyard mentioned here has only two rows even if with three vines (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah, based on the Jerusalem Talmud).

and likewise a large vineyard in which between each row was eight cubits or more has no machol. For it is permitted to sow in it between the rows as above halakhah 3, and all the more so there is no forbidding around it (Radbaz).

and it does not have a width of four handbreadths, it has no machol. For only a fence of such thickness is considered an important fence for this purpose such that four cubits are left beside it unsown (Arukh HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 296:63).
a trench. A channel.

that is ten handbreadths deep and four wide. For a trench they required a width of four handbreadths, since only at such a width is it recognizable, but a fence is recognizable even without such thickness (Arukh HaShulchan, ibid. section 64).
if there is not between one reed and its fellow etc.. For anything less than three handbreadths is considered connected (the law of 'lavud', Hilchot Shabbat 16:17).
many breaches were made in it. And each breach is less than ten cubits.
the standing part. The area that remained fenced.
the partition of the vineyard. Which separates the vineyard from grain or vegetables.
they say to him. The court (Derekh Emunah).
he despaired of it and did not fence it. He gave up fencing it again and put it out of his mind.

he has sanctified. If it grew by half a percent (as above 5:21). And if he is occupied with repairing the breach, he has not sanctified even if it grew by half a percent before he finished the repair (Rik"u and Radbaz).
roofed. With a ceiling.

for the edge of the ceiling is as if it came down and sealed and a partition was made between them. The edge of the ceiling is considered to form a partition beneath it, separating the two parts of the house (see also Hilchot Shabbat 16:7, 17:35).
if he leveled its roofing. He completed the ceiling over all of it.

a small courtyard that was breached in its entirety into a large one etc.. The shared wall of the two courtyards was breached entirely, so that the small courtyard is wholly open to the large one and is considered part of it, while the large courtyard is separated from the small one by a partition (see also Hilchot Tefillah 8:7, Hilchot Eruvin 3:24).
the seeds are forbidden. By the law of one who sows in a vineyard.
and the vines are permitted. For they are separated from the seed by a partition.

if there were vines in the small one, it is permitted to sow in the large one. The large one has no vineyard law (and even though by sowing the large one the small one gets the name 'field', we do not find a prohibition in the Torah against having vines in a field but only a prohibition against seed in a vineyard - Tosafot, Eruvin 92b, s.v. 'gefanim').
posts on this side and that. Parts of wall on both sides of the breach.
open from the head of the vineyard to its head. It crosses the whole vineyard.

and it is permitted to sow in it. For it is not part of the vineyard, and there is no need to keep a distance from the vines either, since the height of the trench has the law of a partition (Derekh Emunah).
as we have explained. Above 6:11.
like a winepress. Like the place for treading grapes.
unless the clearing had sixteen cubits. As above, halakhah 11.
it is like a vineyard destroyed in its middle. As explained above, halakhah 11.
a shomera. A structure or raised mound used for the vineyard watchman to sit.
it is permitted to sow vegetables on top of it. Since it is considered a separate domain.
it must have an empty space of four handbreadths inside it. That the diameter of the shomera be large enough that a square of four by four handbreadths can be squared within it.
so that it is distinct from the ground. A round shomera is recognizable as an independent domain only if it has such a diameter.

and it requires three handbreadths of earth on top of it. A round shomera has an additional stringency: there is no permission to sow on its roof unless there are three handbreadths of earth there for the seeds' nourishment.
the house in the vineyard. A shelter made for plants to protect them from rain or heat (Yad Peshutah).
if it was more than three handbreadths by three handbreadths. And also exactly three handbreadths (Radbaz).

one may sow vegetables inside it. Although the shelter is very small and is not considered an independent domain for sowing on top of it, nevertheless one sows inside it because the vegetable is covered on all sides (Yad Peshutah).
the neka. A hollow for collecting water (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 5:4).
the edge of the trench. The opening of the trench in the ground.

it is forbidden to sow inside it even though he kept six. Since a trench of this size has independent importance and looks like a place made specifically for the vine (Rik"u, Levush, Yoreh De'ah 296:54, Arukh HaShulchan, ibid. section 76).
he shall not sow in the whole enclosure. In the whole fenced area, and the reason is as in the previous halakhah.
and if he kept six and sowed, he did not sanctify. Since by the Torah it suffices to keep six handbreadths (Arukh HaShulchan, ibid.).
as they were created. As created, as is their nature.
the shoots. Thin shoots.
a trellis. A lattice (like a pergola).
and he trained them. He raised the shoots and made an arisa of them.
that is ten high. Handbreadths.
or planted them beside a trench ten deep and four wide. And leaned the shoots on the wall of the trench (channel).

and he must keep away from the arisa... as he keeps away from a vineyard. Although the arisa consists of a single row of vines, and in a vineyard the law of a row of vines is that of a single vine from which one keeps six handbreadths (above 7:1), for an arisa the law is more severe because its shoots spread more, so he keeps four cubits as he does from a vineyard (R. Y. Kafah, based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 6:1).

from the base of the fence over which they trained them. If he wants to sow behind the fence, he must keep four cubits from the fence. And likewise if he wants to sow at the side of the vines, he keeps four cubits from them, as explained shortly.
and it turns out the arisa is from the vines to the wall. The entire area from the vines to the wall is the arisa.
the fence was demolished. Or its height was reduced below ten handbreadths (Radbaz).

an arisa whose middle was destroyed etc.. For example, there were eleven vines planted in a row, and the middle vine was uprooted along with the piece of fence on which it leaned (Yad Peshutah based on the Jerusalem Talmud; and see Rik"u and Radbaz, who explained in other ways).

if there are between them eight cubits and one sixtieth of a cubit. This is the minimum area the vine should leave, if planted by the customary distances of four cubits between vine and vine (see above 7:2), for on each side there are four cubits, and in addition there is the place of the vine itself (Yad Peshutah).

he keeps six handbreadths from each row and sows. He may sow in the destroyed area between the arisot, after keeping six handbreadths from each end, since next to an arisa it suffices to keep six handbreadths (Yad Peshutah).
provided that he does not sow under the epifirot. If epifirot or parts of epifirot remained in the destroyed area, he shall not sow beneath them.
as we have explained. Above 6:12.
eight cubits exactly. Eight cubits precisely.
and if there is no fence there. The fence was entirely destroyed.
he keeps six handbreadths from each row and sows. For a row of vines without a fence has the law of single vines (as above 7:1).

and trained the vines around it on the outside over all its walls. This refers to where each wall has fewer than five vines, since the garden is small, and so there is no real arisa law here but it only looks like an arisa (Radbaz and Yad Peshutah).

if it has enough for a harvester and his basket from here etc.. If on each side of the garden there is room for a person who gathers grapes to stand and room to place his basket (the person's place measures a cubit and the basket's place another cubit - Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 6:1), and additional space remains in the middle of the garden.
and their arisa extends and shades the field. The vines are planted in ground higher than the field, and their branches spread over an arisa and shade an area of the field.
if he stands on the ground and harvests all of it. If it is possible to pick the grapes of the arisa while standing on the ground under the arisa.

we see the whole place... and it forbids four cubits etc.. The Sages required keeping four cubits from the edge of the area the arisa shades, just as one must keep four cubits from the place where the vines grow, since this area looks like an area designated for the vines.
it is forbidden to sow only under the arisa. Just as it is forbidden to sow under shoots that extend from the vine (above 6:11).
two walls adjacent to each other etc.. Where their meeting point forms a corner and the row of vines starts from the corner.

and the arisa goes out with the walls from within the corner and ends. The arisa over which the vines are trained extends from the meeting point of the walls and moves away from them to a certain point ('and ends'), then comes back toward one of the walls, so that the arisa looks like a triangle and is trained on one of the walls (Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah, based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 6:7 and the Rambam's diagram there).

and he sows in the place of the end where there is no arisa over it. After keeping the required distance, he may sow between the end of the distance and the vacant wall, for the vacant wall is not part of the arisa.

a vine whose wood rose a little from the ground etc.. The trunk grew slightly upward and then bent and continued to grow parallel to the ground, and at a certain point bent like a knee (arkuva) upward.
six handbreadths. For a single vine.
four cubits. For a vineyard or arisa.

one measures only from the end of the arkuva etc.. If he wants to sow near the place where the trunk resumes growing upward ('end of the arkuva'), he must keep the distance from it. It is not enough that there is the proper distance from the place where the trunk emerges from the ground ('the first root of the vine'), since the end of the arkuva appears to be the place where the vine grows (and regarding keeping a distance from the first root of the vine, it was already explained above 6:8, in the law of a layered vine, that if the root is visible one must keep a distance from it - see Rik"u).
we have already explained. Above 6:11.
the stalks. The stems.
permitted. Since they were sown permissibly and grew permissibly (Radbaz).
and the grain. Crop that grew after he trained the vine over it.
shall be burned. Shall be set on fire.

the roots of the vineyard were coming out etc.. If the vines' roots emerge from the ground and are visible outside, they have the law of a vineyard from which one must keep distance. But the roots of grain are not kilayim in a vineyard, because they are not seed, and the Torah says 'you shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds' (Deuteronomy 22:9; Levush, Yoreh De'ah 296:67).
in a cubit of six handbreadths. About 48 cm (a handbreadth being about 8 cm).
sokhekket. Generous, so that an additional centimeter is added to each cubit (based on Mishnah Berurah 363 note 89).
for one measures precisely only to be stringent. See also Hilchot Shabbat 17:36.
in Syria. The lands conquered by David, which in certain matters have the law of the Land of Israel (Hilchot Terumot 1:3-4).
with the grape seed by a handful toss. With a grape pit all at once, for which in the Land of Israel one receives lashes as above 5:2.

and although it is permitted to sow vegetables etc.. From the outset it is permitted outside the Land to sow vegetables beside the vineyard as explained above. But when one finds a vegetable growing beside a vineyard and does not know if it was sown permissibly (a vegetable beside the vines) or in violation (two kinds of vegetable and a grape pit by a handful toss), it is forbidden to eat this vegetable. And if it is known with certainty that it was not sown that way, it is permitted to eat (Rik"u in the name of the Rosh; and see the poskim and opinions).
and provided that he sees him picking and selling. The prohibition applies only if the buyer saw the seller picking the vegetable from the sides of the vineyard.
as we have explained in Ma'achalot Asurot. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:11-12.
among kinds of sea animals. But in fish breeding does not apply.
that he inserts by hand like a brush in a tube. A comparison to the insertion of the male organ into the female organ.
rebellion lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
to a sahar. A pen.
and it is forbidden for a Jew to give his animal to a gentile to breed it for him. Since descendants of Noah are forbidden to breed animals (Hilchot Melakhim 10:6).
as explained in Ma'achalot Asurot. See Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:13.
and the village dog. A hunting dog raised in a village (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:6).
the ewes. Sheep.
the mule. A creature born from the crossing of a horse and a donkey.
the arod. Wild donkey (ibid.).
and the ramakh. Wild horse (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 8:5).
its testicles inside. Its testicles are not visible from outside.
and the koy. An animal that is doubtfully a wild animal and doubtfully a domesticated animal (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:13, Hilchot Nezirut 2:10-11, Commentary on the Mishnah, Bikkurim 2:8).

a mule whose mother is a donkey etc.. In the Rambam's view there are four different kinds: donkey, horse, a mule born of a donkey and a mare, and a mule born of a horse and a she-donkey. Each of these four kinds is kilayim by the Torah with each of the other three kinds (Yad Peshutah).
to pull with two mules. To pull a wagon with them, which is prohibited if they are two kinds as brought in the following halakhot.
anywhere. Even outside the Land.

and even if he pulled them as one or led them as one. That the two animals were under one yoke or attached to one wagon or tied with one rope and the like, and he caused them to go together by pulling or in another way ('leading them').
and even by voice. That he caused them to go by speech alone.
and even by voice he receives lashes. Since speech that causes an action has the law of an action (Rik"u and Radbaz).
as it says 'together' in any case. In all ways, even if they are not plowing together.
the one who pairs them. One who ties the animals with one rope and the like.
as we have explained in Ma'achalot Asurot. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 6:1.
shibbut. Apparently this refers to a large fish about a meter and a half long, called in Arabic shabbut.
who were pulling it as kilayim. That it is pulled by two animals which are kilayim with each other.
an animal of disqualified consecrated animals. That was consecrated for a sacrifice and afterwards was disqualified because of a blemish.
like two bodies. Like two different animals.
becomes like sacred and unconsecrated mixed together. Although it was forbidden to offer, it still has certain laws of sanctity.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.
that it speaks only of disqualified consecrated animals. That the word 'tamei' in this verse is not in its usual sense but means disqualified for sacrifice (see also Hilchot Arachin Vacharamin 5:11).
one who breeds with it. With another animal, even of the same kind.
receives lashes for kilayim. In addition to the prohibition of me'ilah with sacred items (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9).
from words of tradition. A law received by tradition.
in coastal cities. In cities near the sea.

like wool that grows on the stones of the Salt Sea. A substance like wool that grows on the stones in the Great Sea (called in our time the Mediterranean; see Hilchot Arachin Vacharamin 8:8 according to the accurate versions).
its form. Its appearance.
and kalakh is its name. A kind of silk (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:2).
ewes. Sheep.
the shirayim. Another kind of silk, resembling flax, and therefore forbidden with kalakh, which resembles wool, and all the more so forbidden with wool itself (Rik"u, Kesef Mishneh and others).
a ewe the daughter of a goat. A goat whose offspring resembles a sheep.
one does not give lashes for it as kilayim. For there is no Torah prohibition except for sheep's wool.
any kind of connection in the world. Any connection at all.

this is kilayim by the Torah. For the prohibition of kilayim of garments is called in the Torah 'shatnez' (Deuteronomy 22:11), and the Sages derived that wool and linen become shatnez through connecting them in one of the ways hinted at in this word: 'shu'a', connection by smoothing; 'tavui', making threads; 'nuz', weaving (Mishnah Kilayim 9:8 and Commentary on the Mishnah there, according to the later edition).
that he mixed them. He mixed them together.
and he shu'a'd them and made felts of them. He smoothed and pressed them together, and made a kind of fabric of them, not by weaving but by the pressure of compacting - this is 'shu'a'.

he joined them and spun them as one and wove a garment of this thread. He joined them by spinning and wove fabric from them - this is 'tavui' and 'nuz' (although a connection by 'tavui' alone is also considered connection, the prohibition of kilayim applies only to garments that are used for warmth, as below halakhah 19, and usually threads that are not woven into a garment are not used for warmth - Derekh Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
he sewed a garment of wool etc.. For sewing, tying and the like are included in weaving.
even if he sewed them with silk. He sewed the wool and flax with silk thread.
he twisted them. He twisted wool and flax threads together and made a thicker thread.

even if he put wool and flax in a sack or basket and bound them. He tied the sack or basket so that it cannot be opened without untying the knot. In this way they are considered connected, and so it is forbidden to put the sack or basket on the body in a way that one is warmed by them (Derekh Emunah).

and even if he tied a wool cord to a flax cord, though the strap is in the middle. Even though the wool and flax are connected by a leather strap between them and do not touch each other, they are kilayim, and it is forbidden to wear such a belt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:9).

for the verse needed to permit kilayim in tzitzit etc.. From the fact that the Torah needed to permit kilayim in tzitzit, though the connection between the wool (the techelet thread) and linen (the garment obligated in tzitzit) in tzitzit is only by tying, we learn that connection by tying too is forbidden by the Torah.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verses.
the passage of kilayim was juxtaposed to the passage of tzitzit. In Deuteronomy 22:11-12.
for he does not diminish the Torah etc.. There is no need to learn from the verses a permission regarding something that is not forbidden by the Torah.
and spun threads from them. He made threads from them.
for the appearance of the whole is the appearance of camel wool. The general appearance of the mixture is camel wool.
to fibers of wool. Thin fibers that have no importance.
and one does not worry about fibers of wool. We do not worry about wool fibers that remained attached to the hide.
the kinbes. A plant from which threads resembling flax are made (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:1).
that he mixed with one another. And afterwards made threads of them.
that was torn. That was ripped.

it is permitted to stitch it with a flax thread and tie. It is permitted to wrap the two sides of the tear with a flax thread that holds both, and to tie the thread. In this way the garment is not considered connected to the thread, since the tears can be removed without untying the knot (Kesef Mishneh and Tur, Yoreh De'ah 300, in the name of the Rosh).
a person may wear a wool garment and a linen garment. One on top of the other.
and gird over them on the outside. It is permitted to tighten them with a belt, since only a connection between the garments themselves is considered a connection.
provided he does not mix etc.. That he not mix a strap from one garment with a strap from the second garment and tie them together (Tosefta Kifshuta, Kilayim 5:15).
a thread. A thread.
and kesatot. Cushions intended for reclining (Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 8:3).
the curtain (parokhet). A drape.
forbidden. For use.
the attendant. The servant, who sometimes warms himself in the curtain.
a shoe that is kilayim and has no heel. A shoe composed only of a sole and laces, which does not cover the back of the foot, and the sole has kilayim in it (R. Y. Kafah).
for the skin of the foot. The skin on the bottom of the foot.
tailors of cloth sew in their usual way etc.. Craftsmen who sew kilayim garments for gentiles may place the garments on their knees as tailors do, if they do not intend to benefit from the garment.
and the scrupulous. Those who are careful about commandments.
sew on the ground. They sew with the garment lying on the ground (or on a table).

sellers sell in their usual way etc.. They place the garment on the shoulder as sellers do, because this placement is not a way of wearing and the benefit from it is not certain (Responsa Birkat Avraham no. 19, Kesef Mishneh).
they hang on a stick. They carry on their shoulders a stick on which the garments are hung (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:5).

for he benefits from the kilayim because of the heat. The garment protects his hand from being burned by the heat of the egg, and such benefit is considered like the benefit of wearing a garment that protects the body from heat or cold (Kesef Mishneh).
or because of the cold. In cold days, when he warms himself by means of the garment (ibid.).
casually. Randomly, for a short time.
to steal the customs. To avoid the property tax that was taken at border crossings, which was not taken on garments a person was wearing.
and if he wore it thus, he receives lashes. For wearing in the manner of wearing is forbidden by the Torah even if he does not benefit from the garment.
small tzaltzulim that people make in their cuffs. Like small pockets attached to the end of the sleeve.
to tie coins in them. To put coins in them.
a plaster (reti'ah). A bandage containing ointment (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:13).
a poultice (melugma). A chewed food placed on the skin for medicine.
an aspelanit. An ointment (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 19:2).
a tzitz. A kind of band on the forehead.
hanging. Dangling.
it is permitted even if he winds them around his hand. For there is no kilayim in this connection.
that are used for wiping. That are used to wipe.
that are used for drying. That are used to dry.
and the barbers' cloths. That barbers place on a person getting a haircut.
markers. Signs sewn on a garment.
and the weavers. The weavers.
in one stitch. In one insertion of a needle with thread into the garments.
it is not a connection. For if he lifts one of the garments, the other slips away immediately.
he gathered the two ends of the thread together. He joined the garments with one stitch and afterwards tied the ends of the thread to each other.
this is kilayim. For a connection of a stitch and a knot, or two stitches even without a knot, is considered sufficiently durable for the prohibition of kilayim.
and sits on it. Since it is hard, and as above halakhah 13.
even to carry manure on it. For he is not wearing it as a garment but placing a load on it.
a mardea. A kind of rug placed under a saddle.
in which a linen thread was lost. That is not visible from the outside.
and pulls it out. He removes the thread that got mixed in.
and we have already explained in Issurei Bi'ah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:17.

and therefore they were lenient in this doubt. Although generally the Sages rule stringently in a doubt about a Torah prohibition, here they ruled leniently, since he tested by dyeing and there is a reasonable basis to assume that the thread slipped out (Radbaz).

and tears it on him. Some inferred from the wording here that he does not strip him completely but tears the garment and leaves it torn on his fellow, since a torn garment is not a way of wearing, thereby saving him from a Torah prohibition (Yad Peshutah).

and why is it set aside for returning a lost item, as will be explained. In Hilchot Gezelah Va'avedah (11:13) it says that an honorable person is not obligated to deal with a lost item he finds if it is beneath his dignity. Although the commandment of returning a lost item is from the Torah, it is set aside because of human dignity.

because it is a prohibition regarding money. Since the commandment of returning a lost item concerns the money of one's fellow, the Torah permitted setting it aside when it harms a person's dignity (see Meiri, Megillah 3a, cited in Yad Peshutah).

and why is it set aside for corpse impurity. The prohibition on a nazir and a kohen to become impure to the dead is set aside when one sees a corpse on the road that has no one to bury it (a 'met mitzvah'; Hilchot Nezirut 7:12, Hilchot Avel 3:8). Apparently the reason is the dignity of the dead person.

since the verse specified 'and for his sister' etc.. The Torah writes a general prohibition on a nazir to become impure to the dead, and then adds a specification of certain people to whom he may not become impure (Numbers 6:6-7). The Sages received by tradition that the specification regarding his sister was written to teach us that specifically for his sister he may not become impure, but he does become impure for a met mitzvah.
it is set aside because of human dignity everywhere. See for example Hilchot Shabbat 26:23.

this prohibition is set aside from its general rule because of human dignity. The command 'do not turn aside' concerns obeying the words of the Sages, and since the Sages themselves teach that their words are set aside for human dignity, the command 'do not turn aside' does not exist at all ('is set aside from its general rule') in a case of human dignity.
he does not tear it on him in the market. He does not tear it on his fellow.
and does not strip in the market. If he discovered that he himself is wearing shatnez.
he receives only one. One series of thirty-nine lashes.
he is liable for each and every one. He is liable for a series of lashes for each time he put his head back in, if he was warned before he put it back.

when is this said etc.. Even a person who wears kilayim continuously all day can incur many lashes if he is warned many times, and after each warning he stayed long enough to be able to take the garment off completely (and not merely take his head out - Rik"u) and put it on again.
one who dresses his fellow etc.. See also Hilchot Nezirut 5:20, Hilchot Avel 3:5.
because of the avnet, which is kilayim. Which was made of linen and embroidered with wool (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:1).

and it was permitted in them only at the time of service etc.. The prohibition of kilayim was permitted to the priests only while performing the commandment of service in the Temple, and so they are forbidden to wear the avnet when not at service (see also ibid. halakhot 11-12).
like tzitzit. Which sets aside the prohibition of kilayim (Hilchot Tzitzit 3:6).
